questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 17 weeks' gestation has a markedly elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). She takes valproic acid for epilepsy and took no supplements before pregnancy. Ultrasound shows the top of the fetal skull is missing and there is no brain tissue where the cerebral hemispheres should be.
questions.leadIn: This malformation results from failure of which of the following?

options.text: Closure of the rostral end of the neural tube during week 4
Closure of the caudal end of the neural tube during week 4
Closure of the rostral end of the neural tube during week 8
Secondary neurulation from the tail bud
Formation of the skull vault after normal neural tube closure

questions.explanation: This is anencephaly. The neural tube closes in the fourth week, and anencephaly results when its rostral (head) end fails to close, around days 23 to 26. Without closure, the skull vault and most of the brain do not form, and the condition is not compatible with life. Maternal serum AFP is markedly raised in about 90% of cases, and amniotic fluid shows high AFP plus acetylcholinesterase. Folic acid at 0.4 mg a day or more before conception lowers the risk, especially in women taking antiseizure drugs. Valproate is the most teratogenic antiseizure drug and interferes with folate absorption.

whyWrong.b: Failure to close the caudal (tail) end causes spina bifida, the other main type of neural tube defect.
whyWrong.c: The neural tube closes in week 4, not week 8.
whyWrong.d: Secondary neurulation from the tail bud forms the lowest (sacral and coccygeal) part of the cord, not the brain.
whyWrong.e: Anencephaly starts with failed closure of the rostral neural tube. The missing skull vault comes with missing brain tissue, so the problem is not the skull alone.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a slow, coarse tremor of his right hand that is worst at rest, eases when he reaches for objects, and stops during sleep. He moves slowly and has trouble getting out of chairs. He is started on levodopa combined with carbidopa.
questions.leadIn: What is the main reason for adding carbidopa?

options.text: It blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine
It directly activates dopamine receptors in the basal ganglia
It inhibits monoamine oxidase B, which breaks down dopamine in the brain
It inhibits catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) to treat end-of-dose wearing off
It blocks muscarinic receptors to reduce tremor

questions.explanation: A resting tremor of one hand with slowness is typical of Parkinson disease. Pigmented dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra degenerate, and Lewy bodies filled with alpha-synuclein form. Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is turned into dopamine in the brain. Outside the brain, the enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase converts it early. Carbidopa is a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor. It stops that early conversion, which lowers the levodopa dose needed to reach the brain. If peripheral side effects such as nausea, vomiting, or light-headedness on standing dominate, more carbidopa can help.

whyWrong.b: Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole directly activate dopamine receptors.
whyWrong.c: MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline and rasagiline block dopamine breakdown in the brain.
whyWrong.d: COMT inhibitors such as entacapone block breakdown of levodopa and dopamine and are added when doses wear off early.
whyWrong.e: Anticholinergic drugs such as benztropine and trihexyphenidyl work best on tremor. Because of side effects in older adults, they are mostly used in younger patients.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman suddenly develops weakness of her left leg, much worse than in her left arm. Her face is not affected. Her family says she has become apathetic and confused, and she has had urinary incontinence since the event. Language is normal.
questions.leadIn: Occlusion of which of the following arteries is most likely?
questions.explanation: An anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke causes weakness on the opposite side that is worst in the leg, plus urinary incontinence, apathy, confusion, poor judgment, and sometimes a grasp reflex or gait apraxia. Her left-sided weakness points to the right hemisphere.

whyWrong.b: Middle cerebral artery strokes cause opposite-side weakness worse in the face and arm than the leg, with aphasia (dominant side) or neglect (nondominant side).
whyWrong.c: A left ACA stroke would weaken the right leg.
whyWrong.d: Posterior cerebral artery strokes cause an opposite-side homonymous hemianopia and memory loss.
whyWrong.e: Lenticulostriate (lacunar) strokes cause pure motor or pure sensory syndromes with no cortical signs such as apathy or incontinence.

sources.title: MSD Manual Professional: Overview of Stroke

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has had brief spells of spinning for 2 weeks. They start when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to reach a high shelf, and each lasts less than a minute. Her hearing is normal, and she has no ringing in her ears. Neurologic examination is normal. With her head turned 45 degrees to the right, she is quickly laid back so her head hangs slightly below the table. After about 10 seconds she feels the room spin, and torsional, upbeating nystagmus appears and fades within 30 seconds.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains her symptoms?

options.text: Loose otoconia moving within a semicircular canal
Excess endolymph distending the inner ear
A schwannoma of the vestibulocochlear nerve

questions.explanation: Answer: loose otoconia in a semicircular canal. Why: short spells of vertigo (less than 1 minute) set off by head position, with normal hearing and a normal neurologic exam, are benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Otoconia (ear crystals) break loose from the utricle and move into a semicircular canal, so moving the head makes the canal fluid move abnormally. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver diagnoses posterior canal BPPV: torsional, upbeating nystagmus with vertigo, after a delay of about 5 to 20 seconds, that fatigues with repeated testing. Treatment is a repositioning maneuver (Epley or Semont), which moves the particles back to the utricle.

whyWrong.b: Excess endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops) is Meniere disease, with attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours plus low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness. Her hearing is normal and her spells last under a minute.
whyWrong.c: Vestibular neuritis causes one continuous attack of vertigo lasting several days, often after a viral illness, not brief spells set off by head movement.
whyWrong.d: A vestibular schwannoma typically causes tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, and imbalance. Her hearing is normal and she has no tinnitus.
whyWrong.e: A fixed stapes footplate is otosclerosis, which causes conductive hearing loss, not positional vertigo.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has had four attacks of severe spinning vertigo with nausea over the past 3 months. Each attack lasts 2 to 4 hours. During attacks his left ear feels full and he hears a low, roaring sound in it. Between attacks his hearing in the left ear seems a little worse each time. An audiogram shows sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear at low and middle frequencies. Neurologic examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his symptoms?

options.text: Excess endolymph distending the inner ear
Loose otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
Abnormal bone fixing the stapes footplate
A Schwann cell tumor on cranial nerve VIII

questions.explanation: Answer: endolymphatic hydrops (Meniere disease). Why: definite Meniere disease needs 2 or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, with low- to mid-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear and fluctuating ear symptoms. A low-pitched, roaring tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the ear are typical. The main tissue finding is endolymphatic hydrops, an excess of endolymph in the inner ear. First-line care is sodium restriction (about 1,500 to 2,300 mg a day) with less caffeine and alcohol, and oral diuretics such as thiazides.

whyWrong.b: Loose otoconia cause BPPV: spells of under a minute set off by head position, with normal hearing.
whyWrong.c: Vestibular neuritis causes one continuous episode of vertigo lasting days, usually after a viral illness, and hearing is normal.
whyWrong.d: Otosclerosis fixes the stapes and causes slowly worsening conductive hearing loss, not attacks of vertigo with sensorineural loss.
whyWrong.e: A vestibular schwannoma causes slowly progressive one-sided sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance rather than discrete attacks of vertigo lasting hours.

questions.topic: Vertigo: vestibular neuritis vs central causes
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had constant spinning vertigo, nausea, and vomiting for 2 days. It began over a few hours, 1 week after a cold. She can walk with help. Hearing is normal in both ears, and she has no headache. She has horizontal nystagmus that always beats to the left, whichever way she looks. When her head is turned quickly to the right, her eyes slip and then make a corrective jerk back to the target. There is no vertical eye misalignment on cover testing, and the rest of the neurologic examination is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: vestibular neuritis. Why: one continuous attack of vertigo that builds over hours, peaks in 24 to 48 hours, and lasts several days, after a viral illness and with normal hearing, is vestibular neuritis, which is presumed to be viral. The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) separates peripheral from central causes. A corrective saccade on head impulse testing points to a peripheral cause, and spontaneous horizontal nystagmus that beats in only one direction is a peripheral sign. Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, a positive test of skew, or other neurologic signs point to a central cause such as stroke.

whyWrong.b: Labyrinthitis has the same vertigo plus one-sided hearing loss. Her hearing is normal.
whyWrong.c: BPPV causes spells of less than 1 minute set off by head position, not constant vertigo for days.
whyWrong.d: Meniere disease causes repeated attacks lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours with low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness.
whyWrong.e: A cerebellar stroke usually causes truncal instability, trouble walking, dysarthria, or other focal signs, with central eye findings such as vertical or direction-changing nystagmus or a positive test of skew. Her head impulse test is abnormal (a peripheral sign) and her exam is otherwise normal.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had slowly worsening hearing in her right ear for 2 years. It got noticeably worse during her pregnancy last year. Her mother needed hearing aids by age 40. The ear canals and tympanic membranes look normal. A vibrating tuning fork placed on the middle of her forehead sounds louder in the right ear. On the right, she hears the fork longer on the mastoid bone than beside the ear canal. On the left, she hears it longer beside the ear canal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hearing loss?

options.text: Abnormal bone fixing the stapes footplate
Noise damage to cochlear hair cells
A Schwann cell tumor on the right cranial nerve VIII
Excess endolymph in the right inner ear
Age-related loss of hair cells in both cochleas

questions.explanation: Answer: otosclerosis. Why: her tests show conductive hearing loss in the right ear. In conductive loss, the Weber test lateralizes to the affected ear, and the Rinne test is negative (bone conduction is better than air conduction) on that side. Otosclerosis replaces dense ear bone with spongy bone that later hardens and fixes the stapes footplate. It usually starts in the third and fourth decades, is about twice as common in women, often runs in families, and can worsen in pregnancy. The tympanic membrane looks normal. Treatment is stapedotomy or stapedectomy with a prosthesis, or hearing aids.

whyWrong.b: Noise damages hair cells and causes sensorineural loss. Then the Weber test lateralizes to the better ear and the Rinne test stays positive (air conduction better than bone) in the affected ear.
whyWrong.c: A vestibular schwannoma causes sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus and imbalance, so the Weber test would go to the left ear.
whyWrong.d: Endolymphatic hydrops (Meniere disease) causes attacks of vertigo with low-frequency sensorineural loss, not slowly progressive conductive loss.
whyWrong.e: Age-related loss is sensorineural and affects both ears in older people; she is 28 with a one-sided conductive pattern.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has had worsening headaches for 3 weeks. His wife says he has become apathetic and forgetful, and he now has weakness of the left arm. MRI shows a large mass in the right frontal lobe with an irregular rim of contrast enhancement around a necrotic center and surrounding edema. A stereotactic biopsy is done.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on the biopsy?

options.text: Whorls of meningothelial cells with psammoma bodies
Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies
Sheets of small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes
Nodules of wet keratin with calcification

questions.explanation: Answer: pseudopalisading necrosis with microvascular proliferation. Why: an enhancing, necrotic mass in a 64-year-old is most likely glioblastoma, which is diagnosed at a median age of 64. High mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis are its hallmarks, and foci of pseudopalisading necrosis are considered pathognomonic. Standard treatment is surgical resection followed by radiation with temozolomide (the Stupp protocol), and median survival is only about 15 months. Recent change: your notes call it "glioblastoma multiforme (grade IV astrocytoma)". The 2021 WHO classification uses "glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype" (CNS WHO grade 4). Tumors with an IDH mutation are now called "astrocytoma, IDH-mutant" and graded 2 to 4.

whyWrong.b: Whorls of meningothelial cells with psammoma bodies are meningioma, a dural-based tumor that enhances evenly.
whyWrong.c: Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies are pilocytic astrocytoma, a mostly childhood tumor that is often a cerebellar cyst with an enhancing nodule.
whyWrong.d: Small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes are medulloblastoma, a cerebellar tumor of young children.
whyWrong.e: Wet keratin with calcification is adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, a suprasellar tumor.

sources.title: Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System: a summary. Neuro-Oncology 2021;23(8):1231-1251

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman had a first seizure. For a year she has had slowly worsening headaches. As a child she received radiation to the head for leukemia. MRI shows a well-circumscribed mass outside the brain tissue, attached to the dura over the left frontal convexity. It enhances evenly with contrast and has a tapering thickening of the adjacent dura.
questions.leadIn: This tumor most likely arose from which of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Answer: arachnoid cap cells. Why: an evenly enhancing, dural-based mass with a dural tail is a meningioma. It usually comes from meningothelial arachnoid cap cells. It is more common in women (about 2.3 to 1), and the mean age at diagnosis is about 66. On histology it forms whorls of meningothelial cells, which can mineralize into psammoma bodies. The meninges are very sensitive to radiation, so prior head radiation raises the risk. Changes on chromosome 22, as in neurofibromatosis type 2, are also linked to meningioma.

whyWrong.b: Astrocytes give rise to tumors within the brain tissue, such as glioblastoma and pilocytic astrocytoma, not dural-based masses.
whyWrong.c: Schwann cells give rise to schwannomas, such as vestibular schwannomas on cranial nerve VIII.
whyWrong.d: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and give rise to ependymomas, which in NF2 occur inside the spinal cord.
whyWrong.e: Oligodendrocytes give rise to oligodendrogliomas, which grow within the brain tissue rather than from the dura.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has had morning headaches and vomiting for 6 weeks, and he has become clumsy. He has a wide-based gait and past-pointing on finger-to-nose testing on the right. MRI shows a mass in the right cerebellar hemisphere made of a large cyst with a brightly enhancing nodule in its wall. The mass is completely removed.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following findings is most likely on histologic examination?
questions.explanation: Answer: Rosenthal fibers. Why: a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellum of a child is a pilocytic astrocytoma. About 75% occur before age 20, most often in the cerebellum, optic pathways, and hypothalamus. Histology shows Rosenthal fibers (elongated eosinophilic bundles) and eosinophilic granular bodies, and the tumor stains for GFAP. BRAF changes are found in 70% to 75% of cases. Complete removal is usually curative: the 10-year survival is about 95%, and recurrence is rare.

whyWrong.b: Pseudopalisading necrosis is the hallmark of glioblastoma, a tumor of older adults.
whyWrong.c: Homer Wright rosettes in small round blue cells suggest medulloblastoma, which is usually solid and arises in the fourth ventricle region.
whyWrong.d: Psammoma bodies in meningothelial whorls are meningioma, a dural-based tumor.
whyWrong.e: Wet keratin is a feature of adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, a calcified suprasellar tumor.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl has had morning vomiting and headaches for 3 weeks and now walks with a wide-based, unsteady gait. Fundoscopy shows papilledema. MRI shows a solid, enhancing midline mass filling the fourth ventricle, with enlarged lateral and third ventricles. MRI of the spine shows several small enhancing nodules along the surface of the spinal cord.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: medulloblastoma. Why: a solid mass in the fourth ventricle region of a young child, with obstructive hydrocephalus and nodules along the spinal cord (drop metastases), is medulloblastoma. It is a WHO grade 4 embryonal tumor that usually arises in the cerebellum in children younger than 10. Because most tumors arise in the fourth ventricle, many children present with obstructive hydrocephalus. It spreads through the CSF to the brain and spinal cord. Histology shows a small, round, blue-cell tumor; Homer Wright rosettes are seen in less than half of samples.

whyWrong.b: Pilocytic astrocytoma is also a cerebellar tumor of children, but it is typically a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule, and complete removal is usually curative.
whyWrong.c: Craniopharyngioma is a calcified, cystic suprasellar tumor that affects vision and pituitary hormones.
whyWrong.d: Glioblastoma is a tumor of older adults (median age 64), usually in the cerebral hemispheres.
whyWrong.e: Meningioma is a dural-based tumor of older adults (mean age about 66).

questions.stem: An 11-year-old boy has headaches and keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. He has grown only 2 cm in the past 2 years and is now below the 3rd percentile for height. He drinks large amounts of water and gets up at night to urinate. Visual field testing shows loss of the outer (temporal) half of the field in both eyes. CT shows a cystic suprasellar mass with calcifications. At surgery the cyst contains yellow-brown, cholesterol-rich fluid.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely on histologic examination of the solid part of the tumor?
questions.explanation: Answer: wet keratin. Why: a calcified, cystic suprasellar mass in a child, with bitemporal field loss, poor growth, and polyuria, is a craniopharyngioma. It arises from remnants of Rathke's pouch, the embryonic outpouching that forms the anterior pituitary. Incidence peaks at ages 5 to 14 and 50 to 74, and 95% have a suprasellar part. Pressure on the optic chiasm causes temporal field loss. Many patients have growth hormone deficiency, and about 20% have vasopressin deficiency (diabetes insipidus). The adamantinomatous type, seen mainly in children, is calcified in about 90% of cases, contains nodules of wet keratin, and has cholesterol-rich cyst fluid.

whyWrong.b: Rosenthal fibers point to pilocytic astrocytoma, usually a cerebellar cyst with a mural nodule.
whyWrong.c: Homer Wright rosettes in small blue cells point to medulloblastoma in the fourth ventricle region.
whyWrong.d: Pseudopalisading necrosis is the hallmark of glioblastoma in older adults.
whyWrong.e: Psammoma bodies in meningothelial whorls are meningioma, a dural-based tumor of older adults.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had ringing in both ears and worsening hearing for 1 year, and he feels unsteady in the dark. His father had surgery for several brain and spinal tumors. Hearing testing shows sensorineural loss in both ears. MRI shows enhancing masses on both vestibulocochlear nerves at the cerebellopontine angles, and a dural-based mass over the right parietal lobe.
questions.leadIn: Loss of which of the following proteins most likely explains his tumors?
questions.explanation: Answer: merlin. Why: bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). NF2 is caused by mutations in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 (22q12.2), which makes merlin, a tumor suppressor. It can be inherited as autosomal dominant (as here, from his father) or arise as a new mutation. Patients typically present with tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, and balance problems. About 50% develop meningiomas (like his dural-based mass), and ependymomas can grow inside the spinal cord. Cataracts are part of the diagnostic criteria. Recent change: in 2022 an international consensus group retired the name "neurofibromatosis 2". GeneReviews now calls the condition NF2-related schwannomatosis, the term that consensus proposed. Older books and some exam questions still use NF2.

whyWrong.b: Neurofibromin is lost in neurofibromatosis type 1, which causes café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and armpit and groin freckling, not bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
whyWrong.c: Loss of the VHL protein causes von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, with hemangioblastomas and kidney cancer rather than schwannomas.
whyWrong.d: Activating RET mutations cause MEN 2 (medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma).
whyWrong.e: Loss of dystrophin causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a muscle disease.

sources.title: Plotkin SR et al. Updated diagnostic criteria and nomenclature for neurofibromatosis type 2 and schwannomatosis. Genet Med 2022;24(9):1967-1977

questions.stem: A 21-year-old college student notices that the whites of his eyes are yellow during final exams week, after he skipped meals for 2 days. He feels well. Total bilirubin is 3.0 mg/dL, with direct (conjugated) bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL. ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, and LDH are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his jaundice?

options.text: A stone blocking the common bile duct

questions.explanation: Answer: reduced UGT1A1 activity (Gilbert syndrome). Why: mild, isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin usually below 4 mg/dL) with normal liver enzymes and no hemolysis is Gilbert syndrome. UGT1A1 works at only 30% to 50% of normal, so less bilirubin is conjugated. It is autosomal recessive. Fasting, febrile illness, menstruation, and physical exertion are common triggers. No treatment is needed. One drug point: irinotecan is well known to cause toxicity in people with Gilbert syndrome.

whyWrong.b: Absent UGT1A1 is Crigler-Najjar type 1, which causes severe unconjugated jaundice in newborns with a high risk of kernicterus.
whyWrong.c: A defective MRP2 transporter is Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which raises conjugated (direct) bilirubin. His bilirubin is mostly unconjugated.
whyWrong.d: Hemolysis would raise the reticulocyte count and LDH, which are normal.
whyWrong.e: Bile duct obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman notices mild yellowing of her eyes 2 months after starting an oral contraceptive. She feels well and has no itching or abdominal pain. Total bilirubin is 4.1 mg/dL, with direct (conjugated) bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL. ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT are normal. Ultrasound shows a normal liver and bile ducts.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following findings is most likely on further evaluation?

options.text: Normal total urinary coproporphyrin, with more than 80% as isomer I
An unconjugated bilirubin level that falls after phenobarbital
Beading of the bile ducts on cholangiography

questions.explanation: Answer: normal total urinary coproporphyrin, more than 80% isomer I. Why: a mild, mostly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes and normal bile ducts, unmasked by oral contraceptives, is Dubin-Johnson syndrome. Mutations in ABCC2 impair MRP2, the transporter that moves conjugated bilirubin out of liver cells into bile. Oral contraceptives, illness, and pregnancy can trigger jaundice. A liver biopsy, if done, shows dark, coarsely granular pigment in centrilobular hepatocytes. Total urinary coproporphyrin is normal, but more than 80% is isomer I, a pattern not seen in Rotor syndrome. It is benign, does not cause cirrhosis, and needs no treatment.

whyWrong.b: A fall in unconjugated bilirubin with phenobarbital fits Crigler-Najjar type 2. Her raised bilirubin is mostly conjugated.
whyWrong.c: Antimitochondrial antibodies point to primary biliary cholangitis, which raises alkaline phosphatase and GGT and causes itching. Her cholestatic enzymes are normal.
whyWrong.d: A high reticulocyte count means hemolysis, which raises unconjugated bilirubin, not conjugated.
whyWrong.e: Beaded ducts on cholangiography are primary sclerosing cholangitis, which raises alkaline phosphatase. Her ducts and enzymes are normal.

questions.stem: A 4-day-old boy, born at term to parents who are first cousins, has deep jaundice. Total bilirubin is 26 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative, and hemoglobin and reticulocyte count are normal. Intensive phototherapy is started. A 2-week trial of phenobarbital does not lower his bilirubin, and he still needs phototherapy many hours every day at 2 months of age.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his jaundice?

options.text: Fibrous obliteration of the bile ducts

questions.explanation: Answer: absent UGT1A1 activity. Why: severe unconjugated jaundice from birth, with no hemolysis, that does not respond to phenobarbital is Crigler-Najjar syndrome type 1. UGT1A1 (UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1) activity is absent or minimal, so bilirubin cannot be conjugated. It is autosomal recessive, and consanguinity raises the risk. Infants are at very high risk of kernicterus. The main treatment is intensive daily phototherapy, and liver transplantation is the only cure. In type 2, enzyme activity is reduced rather than absent, bilirubin is usually below 20 mg/dL, and phenobarbital lowers it.

whyWrong.b: Reduced UGT1A1 activity is Gilbert syndrome or Crigler-Najjar type 2. In type 2, bilirubin is usually below 20 mg/dL and phenobarbital lowers it. His bilirubin is 26 mg/dL and did not respond.
whyWrong.c: A defective MRP2 transporter is Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which raises conjugated bilirubin. His is almost all unconjugated.
whyWrong.d: Hemolysis is ruled out: the Coombs test, hemoglobin, and reticulocyte count are normal.
whyWrong.e: Fibrous obliteration of the bile ducts is biliary atresia, which raises conjugated bilirubin and causes pale stools.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old girl has been yellow since her second week of life. Her parents say her stools have become pale, like putty, and her diaper urine is dark. She is feeding well. The liver edge is firm and palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Total bilirubin is 7.8 mg/dL, with direct (conjugated) bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL, and GGT is raised. An intraoperative cholangiogram shows no flow of contrast into the extrahepatic bile ducts.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Observation, because jaundice in infants is usually physiologic
Liver transplantation as the first operation

questions.explanation: Answer: the Kasai procedure. Why: jaundice lasting beyond 2 weeks with pale (acholic) stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Jaundice that persists for more than 14 days is not physiologic and needs prompt evaluation. Intraoperative cholangiography is the diagnostic gold standard. Standard treatment is the Kasai hepatic portoenterostomy, ideally before 60 days of life, because earlier surgery restores bile flow better. Liver transplantation is reserved for a failed Kasai or advanced biliary cirrhosis.

whyWrong.b: Phototherapy lowers unconjugated bilirubin. Her bilirubin is mostly conjugated, from blocked bile flow.
whyWrong.c: Phenobarbital lowers unconjugated bilirubin in Crigler-Najjar type 2; it does not open blocked bile ducts.
whyWrong.d: Jaundice beyond 14 days with pale stools and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiologic.
whyWrong.e: Transplantation is the definitive therapy only after a failed Kasai or with advanced biliary cirrhosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with known gallstones has had fever, chills, and right upper quadrant pain for 1 day. Her temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), pulse 118/min, and blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg. She is confused and her sclerae are yellow. WBC count is 19,000/mm³, total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL (direct 4.8 mg/dL), and alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains her condition?

options.text: Blocked common bile duct with infected bile
Blocked cystic duct with an inflamed gallbladder

questions.explanation: Answer: a blocked common bile duct with infected bile (acute cholangitis). Why: fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice are Charcot triad. Adding confusion and shock gives Reynolds pentad, a sign of severe cholangitis. Cholangitis needs obstruction of bile flow, most often a stone in the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis). Gut bacteria, mainly gram-negative organisms such as E. coli, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter, grow in the trapped bile. Complete obstruction raises the pressure inside the ducts, which often pushes bacteria into the blood, so she is septic. Treatment is antibiotics plus urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP, which works in 94% to 98% of cases.

whyWrong.b: Acute cholecystitis comes from a stone in the cystic duct. That does not dilate the common bile duct or block bile leaving the liver, so it does not explain her dilated common bile duct and high direct bilirubin.
whyWrong.c: A defective MRP2 transporter is Dubin-Johnson syndrome, a mild, benign rise in conjugated bilirubin with normal liver enzymes, not fever and shock.
whyWrong.d: Hemolysis raises unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin. Most of her bilirubin is direct.
whyWrong.e: Reduced UGT1A1 activity is Gilbert syndrome, a mild unconjugated rise (usually below 4 mg/dL) with normal liver enzymes.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy who has received no vaccines developed a high fever and severe sore throat over 6 hours. He is drooling, refuses to swallow, and speaks in a muffled voice. He sits upright, leaning forward on his hands with his neck extended, and looks very ill. He has soft inspiratory stridor and is anxious.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Secure the airway in the operating room with an experienced team
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Give nebulized racemic epinephrine and oral dexamethasone
Lay him flat to place an IV and draw blood cultures
Give oral amoxicillin and recheck in 24 hours

questions.explanation: Answer: secure the airway in a controlled setting. Why: rapid-onset fever with drooling, dysphagia, and distress (the 3 Ds), a muffled "hot potato" voice, and a toxic look in an unvaccinated child is epiglottitis. Haemophilus influenzae type b caused most childhood cases before the Hib vaccine, and H. influenzae is still the single most common cause. Lateral neck x-ray shows a swollen epiglottis (the thumb sign). Because the airway can close suddenly, the airway should ideally be secured in the operating room. Avoid anything that agitates the child, and never use a tongue blade to look in the throat. After the airway is secure, give empiric antibiotics such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or cefuroxime.

whyWrong.b: A tongue blade can trigger complete airway obstruction and should never be used when epiglottitis is suspected.
whyWrong.c: Racemic epinephrine and dexamethasone treat croup. In epiglottitis, unnecessary inhalers, racemic epinephrine, and agitation should be avoided.
whyWrong.d: These children struggle to lie flat and should be handled calmly. Securing the airway comes before painful procedures.
whyWrong.e: Epiglottitis can progress quickly to airway obstruction, so outpatient oral antibiotics are unsafe.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought in during January with 2 days of runny nose followed by cough and fast breathing. Her temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), respiratory rate is 60/min, and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. She has subcostal retractions, and the chest has diffuse wheezes and fine crackles. She is feeding a little less than usual.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Answer: respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Why: an infant under 2 years with a cold that progresses to fast breathing, retractions, wheezing, and fine crackles in winter has bronchiolitis, and RSV causes up to 80% of cases. Care is supportive: oxygen if saturation is low and hydration with small, frequent feeds. Bronchodilators are not reliably effective, and glucocorticoids are not recommended for a first episode. Recent change: your microbiology notes give palivizumab for RSV prevention in premature infants. CDC now protects infants with either a maternal RSV vaccine in pregnancy or a long-acting antibody (nirsevimab or clesrovimab) for babies under 8 months in their first RSV season. Palivizumab is no longer available after December 31, 2025.

whyWrong.b: Parainfluenza virus is the main cause of croup, which presents with a barking cough and inspiratory stridor rather than diffuse wheezes and crackles.
whyWrong.c: H. influenzae type b causes epiglottitis: sudden high fever, drooling, and stridor in a toxic-looking child.
whyWrong.d: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia mainly in children aged 5 to 14 and young adults. Infants younger than 6 months are rarely infected.
whyWrong.e: Group A streptococcus causes pharyngitis, not a wheezy lower respiratory infection in infants.

sources.title: CDC: RSV Immunization Guidance for Infants and Young Children (updated Aug 18, 2025)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy started coughing and choking while eating peanuts at a party yesterday. He now has a cough and audible wheezing. He has no fever. On examination, breath sounds are reduced over the left lung, with wheezing on that side. Chest x-ray in inspiration is normal. Decubitus films show that the left lung stays expanded when he lies on his left side.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Answer: rigid bronchoscopy. Why: sudden choking and coughing while eating, followed by one-sided wheezing and reduced breath sounds, is foreign body aspiration until proven otherwise. Most cases are toddlers (98% are under 5 years). Chest x-rays are often normal; the most common abnormality is air trapping. For children under 5, bilateral decubitus films are preferred: the side with the object does not deflate when it is down. Bronchoscopy both diagnoses and removes the object, and rigid bronchoscopy allows ventilation through the scope and a better view. Note: your notes say aspirated material goes more often to the right main bronchus, which is classic teaching for adults. In children under 15, objects land in the left lung almost as often as in the right, because the angles where the two bronchi branch off are more symmetric.

whyWrong.b: One-sided wheeze after a choking episode is not asthma. Treating with albuterol leaves the object in place.
whyWrong.c: Antibiotics do not remove the object. A retained object can lead to infection later.
whyWrong.d: Waiting allows complications. A normal x-ray does not rule out a foreign body.
whyWrong.e: Chest physiotherapy does not reliably remove an aspirated object and can dislodge it into a worse position.

questions.topic: Newborn breathing trouble: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
questions.stem: A boy is born at 30 weeks' gestation by emergency cesarean delivery to a mother with poorly controlled diabetes. She did not receive corticosteroids before delivery. Within 1 hour he has grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and cyanosis on room air. Chest x-ray shows low lung volumes with a diffuse ground-glass, reticulogranular pattern and air bronchograms.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his condition?

options.text: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid
Meconium blocking the airways and inactivating surfactant
A one-way air leak into the pleural space
Infection of the bronchioles by respiratory syncytial virus

questions.explanation: Answer: surfactant deficiency. Why: a premature newborn with grunting, retractions, and cyanosis soon after birth, and a ground-glass reticulogranular x-ray with air bronchograms, has neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Surfactant is made by alveolar type 2 cells, starting around 20 weeks of gestation, so premature lungs do not have enough. The biggest risk factors are prematurity and low birth weight; others include male sex, late preterm delivery, and maternal diabetes. Antenatal corticosteroids markedly reduce the risk. Treatment is nasal CPAP and surfactant replacement. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is a chronic complication.

whyWrong.b: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid is transient tachypnea of the newborn. It mainly affects term and late-preterm babies, often after cesarean delivery without labor, shows fluid in the fissures on x-ray, and resolves within 24 to 72 hours.
whyWrong.c: Meconium aspiration affects term and post-term babies born through meconium-stained fluid; later films show hyperinflation and atelectasis.
whyWrong.d: A one-way air leak is a tension pneumothorax, which causes one-sided absent breath sounds and a shifted mediastinum, not a diffuse ground-glass pattern.
whyWrong.e: RSV bronchiolitis affects infants after the newborn period, starting with a cold, not a preterm baby within an hour of birth.

sources.title: StatPearls: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being thrown from an all-terrain vehicle. He is gasping and anxious. Pulse is 142/min, blood pressure 74/40 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 84% on a face mask. Breath sounds are absent on the right, and the right chest is hyperresonant to percussion. The trachea is shifted to the left, and the neck veins are distended.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains his hypotension?

options.text: Decreased venous return to the heart
Fluid compressing the heart within the pericardium
Weak pumping by a bruised heart muscle
Blood loss from an injured abdominal organ

questions.explanation: Answer: decreased venous return. Why: absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, a trachea shifted away from the affected side, distended neck veins, and hypotension after chest trauma are a tension pneumothorax. A one-way valve lets air into the pleural space on inspiration but not out on expiration, so pressure builds and pushes the mediastinum to the other side. The high pressure compresses the superior vena cava, so less blood returns to the heart and cardiac output falls. That is why he is hypotensive and his neck veins are distended. The diagnosis is clinical. In an unstable patient, needle decompression is done at once, without waiting for imaging, and a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) follows.

whyWrong.b: Cardiac tamponade also causes distended neck veins and hypotension, but breath sounds are present and the trachea is midline. Heart sounds are muffled, and pulsus paradoxus may be present.
whyWrong.c: Loss of arterial tone (distributive shock, as in sepsis or spinal injury) does not explain absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, and a trachea pushed to the left. His shock is mechanical.
whyWrong.d: A bruised heart can pump poorly after blunt chest trauma, but that would not cause absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, or a shifted trachea.
whyWrong.e: Bleeding from an injured organ causes shock, but it does not explain the one-sided chest findings, and blood loss would not distend the neck veins.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he no longer rolls over or reaches for toys, which he did 2 months ago. He startles violently at ordinary household noises. His parents are of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. He is at the 50th percentile for weight. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. Funduscopic examination shows a cherry-red spot in the macula of each eye.
questions.leadIn: Accumulation of which of the following substances in his neurons is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: GM2 ganglioside (Tay-Sachs disease). Why: loss of milestones at 4 to 6 months, an exaggerated startle to sound, and a cherry-red spot without an enlarged liver or spleen is infantile Tay-Sachs disease. Mutations in HEXA (chromosome 15q23) cause deficiency of hexosaminidase A, so GM2 ganglioside builds up in neuronal lysosomes. Under the electron microscope the lysosomes look like whorled onion-skin layers. It is autosomal recessive and more common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish heritage. Macrocephaly develops by about 18 months, and children with the infantile form usually die by age 4 to 5. Note: your table writes the enzyme as "hexosaminidase"; the full name is hexosaminidase A.

whyWrong.b: Sphingomyelin builds up in Niemann-Pick disease type A. It also gives a cherry-red spot, but the liver and spleen are enlarged.
whyWrong.c: Glucocerebroside builds up in Gaucher disease, which enlarges the liver and spleen and affects bone. There is no cherry-red spot.
whyWrong.d: Galactocerebroside is the substrate of the enzyme missing in Krabbe disease, which causes irritability, feeding problems, and optic atrophy rather than a cherry-red spot.
whyWrong.e: Sulfatide builds up in metachromatic leukodystrophy, which damages myelin and causes walking problems and slowed nerve conduction.

sources.title: MSD Manual Consumer Version: Metachromatic Leukodystrophy (reviewed Mar 2024)

questions.stem: A 5-month-old girl of Ashkenazi Jewish descent is evaluated for poor feeding and a swollen abdomen. She smiled and held her head up at 3 months but now does neither. The liver edge is 6 cm and the spleen tip 5 cm below the costal margins. Funduscopic examination shows a cherry-red spot in the macula of each eye. A bone marrow aspirate shows many large macrophages with foamy, finely vacuolated cytoplasm.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: acid sphingomyelinase (Niemann-Pick disease type A). Why: an infant with neurologic decline, a cherry-red spot, and a large liver and spleen has Niemann-Pick disease type A. Mutations in SMPD1 leave acid sphingomyelinase almost inactive, so sphingomyelin, which it normally breaks into ceramide and phosphocholine, builds up in macrophages. These lipid-laden macrophages are the foam cells seen in the marrow, and they fill the liver, spleen, lungs, and brain. It is autosomal recessive and more common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. Type A is usually fatal in early childhood. Type C is a different defect: loss of NPC1 or NPC2 traps cholesterol inside lysosomes. Recent change: in August 2022 the FDA approved olipudase alfa (Xenpozyme), the first treatment for acid sphingomyelinase deficiency; it treats the symptoms outside the nervous system. StatPearls still lists enzyme replacement as under study.

whyWrong.b: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs disease) also causes a cherry-red spot and loss of milestones, but the liver and spleen are not enlarged.
whyWrong.c: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher disease) enlarges the liver and spleen, but it does not cause a cherry-red spot.
whyWrong.d: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry disease) is X-linked and causes burning pain in the hands and feet, skin angiokeratomas, and kidney disease, usually starting in childhood or later.
whyWrong.e: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe disease) causes irritability and optic atrophy. It is not known for a large liver and spleen or a cherry-red spot.

sources.title: BioSpace: FDA Approves First Treatment for Acid Sphingomyelinase Deficiency (31 Aug 2022)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has had episodes of burning pain in his hands and feet since he was 9 years old. The pain comes on with exercise or hot weather, and he sweats very little. He has clusters of small, dark red papules on his lower abdomen and upper thighs. Slit-lamp examination shows whorl-like opacities in both corneas. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein. His mother's brother started dialysis at age 42.
questions.leadIn: Accumulation of which of the following substances is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: globotriaosylceramide (Fabry disease). Why: painful burning in the hands and feet (acroparesthesias), little sweating (hypohidrosis), angiokeratomas, whorled corneal opacities (corneal verticillata), and protein in the urine are Fabry disease. Low activity of alpha-galactosidase A lets globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) build up in lysosomes. Over time it damages the kidneys, heart, and brain blood vessels, causing kidney failure, heart disease, and strokes. The gene is on the X chromosome, which fits an affected man whose maternal uncle needed dialysis. Heterozygous women usually have a milder course. Treatment includes enzyme replacement infusions every 2 weeks.

whyWrong.b: GM2 ganglioside builds up in Tay-Sachs disease, which causes neurologic decline in infancy, not pain and kidney disease in a young adult.
whyWrong.c: Sphingomyelin builds up in Niemann-Pick disease, with a large liver and spleen and, in type A, early childhood death.
whyWrong.d: Glucocerebroside builds up in Gaucher disease, which enlarges the liver and spleen and affects bone and blood counts.
whyWrong.e: Sulfatide builds up in metachromatic leukodystrophy, which damages myelin and causes walking problems and loss of skills.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has had restlessness, constant irritability, vomiting, and feeding difficulty for 6 weeks and has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile for weight. He now arches his back and neck when handled, and he does not follow faces. Funduscopic examination shows pale optic discs. Nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction. A brain biopsy shows large multinucleated macrophages in the white matter.
questions.leadIn: Accumulation of which of the following toxic metabolites most likely contributes to his condition?
questions.explanation: Answer: psychosine (Krabbe disease, also called globoid cell leukodystrophy). Why: irritability, vomiting, feeding difficulty, and failure to thrive, followed by optic atrophy and opisthotonic posturing, is the infantile form of Krabbe disease. Mutations in GALC (chromosome 14) cause deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramide beta-galactosidase). Psychosine, a toxic lipid made during myelin synthesis, builds up and damages myelin. The multinucleated globoid cells on biopsy give the disease its other name, and nerve conduction is slowed in most infants. It is autosomal recessive. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant works best before symptoms start. Note: your table gives the enzyme as "beta-galactosidase"; the specific enzyme is galactocerebrosidase.

whyWrong.b: Very long-chain fatty acids build up in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, which usually starts at ages 4 to 8 with behavior and school problems and adrenal insufficiency.
whyWrong.c: Homogentisic acid builds up in alkaptonuria, which darkens urine and later causes arthritis. It does not cause infant neurodegeneration.
whyWrong.d: Orotic acid builds up in hereditary orotic aciduria, which causes megaloblastic anemia and failure to thrive, not globoid cells in white matter.
whyWrong.e: Branched-chain amino acids build up in maple syrup urine disease, which causes vomiting, lethargy, and seizures in the first days of life with a maple syrup odor.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl who began walking at 13 months has fallen more and more often over the past 6 months, and she now cannot walk without support. She has also stopped using the few words she had. Her legs are weak. Nerve conduction studies show slowed conduction, and MRI of the brain shows symmetric white matter changes. Urinary sulfatide excretion is increased.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: arylsulfatase A (metachromatic leukodystrophy, MLD). Why: a toddler who loses the ability to walk and talk, with slowed nerve conduction and white matter disease, has a leukodystrophy, and high urinary sulfatides point to MLD. Without arylsulfatase A, sulfatides build up in the white matter of the brain and spinal cord, in nerves, and in other organs, so myelin breaks down and nerves conduct poorly. It is autosomal recessive. The infantile form starts before age 4. Recent change: in March 2024 the FDA approved atidarsagene autotemcel (Lenmeldy), a one-time gene therapy made from the child's own blood stem cells modified to carry working copies of the ARSA gene; all treated children with presymptomatic late-infantile MLD were alive at age 6. MSD (reviewed March 2024) still describes gene therapy as under study. Note: your table writes "arylsulfatase"; the full name is arylsulfatase A.

whyWrong.b: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe disease) usually starts in early infancy with irritability, feeding problems, and optic atrophy, and the biopsy shows globoid cells.
whyWrong.c: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs disease) starts at 3 to 6 months with an exaggerated startle and a cherry-red spot.
whyWrong.d: Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick disease) enlarges the liver and spleen. Raised urinary sulfatides point elsewhere.
whyWrong.e: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry disease) causes burning pain, angiokeratomas, and kidney disease, not loss of walking in a toddler.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has had falling school grades, trouble paying attention, and new behavior problems for 6 months. He has also been more tired than usual. Serum sodium is 129 mEq/L and potassium 5.6 mEq/L. His morning cortisol is low, and his ACTH is high. MRI of the brain shows white matter changes in both hemispheres.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely increased in his plasma?
questions.explanation: Answer: very long-chain fatty acids (X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, X-ALD). Why: a school-age boy with declining school performance and behavior, white matter disease, and primary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol with high ACTH, low sodium, high potassium) has X-ALD. Pathogenic variants in ABCD1 impair breakdown of very long-chain fatty acids in peroxisomes, so they build up; a raised plasma C26:0 (hexacosanoic acid) supports the diagnosis, and finding the ABCD1 variant confirms it. It is X-linked. Childhood cerebral disease most often starts between ages 4 and 8, with a peak at age 7. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant is recommended for early childhood cerebral disease.

whyWrong.b: High phenylalanine is phenylketonuria, which causes intellectual disability from infancy if untreated. It does not cause adrenal insufficiency.
whyWrong.c: High homocysteine is classic homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and blood clots.
whyWrong.d: High branched-chain amino acids (especially leucine) point to maple syrup urine disease, which usually presents in the first days of life with vomiting, lethargy, and seizures.
whyWrong.e: High ammonia points to a urea cycle disorder. Neither that nor the others explain adrenal failure with white matter disease.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he cannot sit without support. He was born at home in a region without newborn screening. He has an eczema-like rash on his cheeks and limbs. His skin, hair, and eyes are much lighter than his parents'. His mother says his urine and sweat have a musty, mousy smell.
questions.leadIn: Deficient activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: phenylalanine hydroxylase (phenylketonuria, PKU). Why: developmental delay, an eczema-like rash, light skin and hair, and a mousy odor are untreated PKU. Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor. When it fails, phenylalanine builds up, and tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid that may need to be supplemented. The hallmark of untreated PKU is severe intellectual disability, and seizures can occur if treatment is late. All newborns are screened 24 to 48 hours after birth. Treatment is lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction, and a trial of sapropterin (synthetic BH4) is recommended. Recent change: on 28 July 2025 the FDA approved sepiapterin (Sephience) for children and adults with PKU, used with a phenylalanine-restricted diet. Your notes list sapropterin, which is still used. Note: some PKU-like cases come from BH4 defects (for example dihydropteridine reductase deficiency), which also disrupt neurotransmitter synthesis.

whyWrong.b: Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency is alkaptonuria: urine that darkens in air, skin pigmentation, and arthritis in adults.
whyWrong.c: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency is tyrosinemia type 1, which affects the liver and is confirmed by high succinylacetone.
whyWrong.d: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and blood clots.
whyWrong.e: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency is maple syrup urine disease, which causes a crisis in the first days of life and a maple syrup odor.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has had worsening low back pain and stiffness and pain in both knees for several years. He has dark gray-blue patches of skin pigmentation on his ears and face. He says his urine has always turned dark brown to black if it sits in a container exposed to air. X-rays show degenerative changes in the lumbar spine and knees.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: homogentisic acid oxidase (alkaptonuria). Why: urine that turns dark when exposed to air, dark skin pigmentation (ochronosis), and arthritis in adulthood are alkaptonuria. It is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine breakdown. Homogentisic acid cannot be broken down, so it is excreted in urine, where it oxidizes and darkens, and it is deposited in tissues. MSD says ascorbic acid may reduce pigment deposition. Recent change: in September 2020 the European Medicines Agency recommended nitisinone (Orfadin) for adults with alkaptonuria, because it lowers homogentisic acid in blood and urine. MSD still says there is no effective treatment.

whyWrong.b: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is phenylketonuria, which causes intellectual disability in childhood if untreated, not dark urine and arthritis in an adult.
whyWrong.c: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency is tyrosinemia type 1, a liver disease of infancy and childhood.
whyWrong.d: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and blood clots.
whyWrong.e: HGPRT deficiency is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, with high uric acid, self-injury, and abnormal movements in boys.

questions.stem: A 5-day-old girl, born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, has had vomiting for 2 days and is now very lethargic. This morning she had a seizure. Her parents are first cousins. Her earwax and urine have a sweet odor like maple syrup. Blood glucose is normal.
questions.leadIn: Plasma levels of which of the following amino acids are most likely increased?
questions.explanation: Answer: leucine (maple syrup urine disease, MSUD). Why: a newborn who becomes severely ill in the first days of life, with vomiting and lethargy progressing to seizures, and body fluids that smell of maple syrup (especially strong in earwax) has MSUD. A defect in the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex blocks breakdown of the branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine. Diagnosis rests on high plasma branched-chain amino acids, particularly leucine. Thiamine is a cofactor, and some patients respond to high-dose thiamine. Long-term treatment restricts branched-chain amino acids in the diet, and liver transplantation is curative. Note: your table names the enzyme "alpha-ketoacid decarboxylase"; MSD names the whole dehydrogenase complex, with thiamine needed for the decarboxylation step, so both point at the same enzyme. Untreated, it progresses to coma and death.

whyWrong.b: High phenylalanine is phenylketonuria, which causes slow developmental delay, not a crisis in the first week.
whyWrong.c: High methionine is the newborn screening marker for classic homocystinuria, which does not cause an acute crisis or a maple syrup odor.
whyWrong.d: High tyrosine points to a tyrosine metabolism disorder such as tyrosinemia, which mainly affects the liver.
whyWrong.e: High homocysteine is homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and blood clots later in childhood.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a painful, swollen left calf, and ultrasound shows a deep vein thrombosis. He has mild intellectual disability. He is of average height but has long, thin limbs. His ophthalmologist recently found that both lenses are partly dislocated. An x-ray taken last year for a wrist fracture showed osteoporosis.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following is most likely increased in his plasma?
questions.explanation: Answer: homocysteine (classic homocystinuria). Why: lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), intellectual disability, osteoporosis, a marfanoid build, and a blood clot at a young age are classic homocystinuria. It is an autosomal recessive deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase. Newborn screening looks for high methionine, and a high total plasma homocysteine confirms the diagnosis. Arterial and venous clots can occur at any age. Patients can have a marfanoid habitus even though they are not usually tall. About half respond to high-dose pyridoxine (vitamin B6) alone; others need a low-methionine diet with cysteine supplements, and betaine helps lower homocysteine. Note: books number the types of homocystinuria differently, so learn each type by its enzyme, not its number.

whyWrong.b: High leucine is maple syrup urine disease, a crisis in the first days of life.
whyWrong.c: High phenylalanine is phenylketonuria, which causes intellectual disability but not lens dislocation or blood clots.
whyWrong.d: High very long-chain fatty acids point to X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, with school decline, white matter disease, and adrenal insufficiency.
whyWrong.e: High uric acid in a boy with abnormal movements and self-injury would suggest Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has delayed motor development and cannot sit without support. He has slow writhing movements of the arms and sustained twisting postures. Over the past few months he has started biting his lips and fingers, causing wounds. His mother remembers orange, sand-like crystals in his diapers when he was an infant. Serum uric acid is 11 mg/dL.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT; Lesch-Nyhan syndrome). Why: a boy with motor delay, dystonia and choreoathetosis, self-injurious biting of the lips and fingers (usually starting at ages 2 to 4), and high uric acid has Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Orange crystals ("orange sand") in the diaper can be the earliest clue. HGPRT recycles purine bases (the salvage pathway). Without it, the cell makes more purines from scratch (de novo), and the excess is broken down to uric acid, which causes gout and kidney stones. The gene, HPRT1, is on the X chromosome, so the disease is X-linked recessive and affects boys. Allopurinol controls uric acid and prevents gout and stones, but it does not improve the neurologic or behavioral symptoms.

whyWrong.b: UMP synthase deficiency is hereditary orotic aciduria, a pyrimidine disorder with megaloblastic anemia and orotic acid crystals, not high uric acid.
whyWrong.c: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is phenylketonuria, with intellectual disability, light skin, and a musty odor.
whyWrong.d: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency is Krabbe disease, a leukodystrophy of early infancy.
whyWrong.e: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and blood clots.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old boy is evaluated for poor weight gain and delayed milestones. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 112 fL, and the blood smear shows megaloblastic changes. Serum vitamin B12 and folate are normal. His urine is cloudy, and urinary orotic acid is markedly increased. Blood ammonia is normal.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
questions.explanation: Answer: UMP synthase (hereditary orotic aciduria). Why: megaloblastic anemia in the first months of life with normal B12 and folate, failure to thrive, developmental delay, and orotic acid crystals in the urine are hereditary orotic aciduria. UMP synthase (uridine 5'-monophosphate synthase) does the last two steps of pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid piles up and cells cannot make enough pyrimidines for DNA. It is autosomal recessive. The key contrast is with urea cycle disorders such as ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, which also raise urinary orotic acid but cause high blood ammonia; hereditary orotic aciduria does not. Treatment is lifelong uridine triacetate (Xuriden), approved by the FDA, which supplies the missing uridine. Note: your notes list uridine or uridine monophosphate; uridine triacetate is the approved form.

whyWrong.b: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency also raises urinary orotic acid, but it causes high blood ammonia. His ammonia is normal.
whyWrong.c: HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) is a purine disorder with high uric acid and self-injury, not megaloblastic anemia.
whyWrong.d: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (phenylketonuria) causes developmental delay but not megaloblastic anemia or orotic aciduria.
whyWrong.e: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency (homocystinuria) causes lens dislocation and blood clots, not orotic aciduria.

questions.stem: A new rapid blood test for a bacterial infection is evaluated in 1,000 patients with fever. Blood culture, the reference standard, shows that 200 have the infection and 800 do not. The rapid test is positive in 180 of the patients with infection and in 40 of the patients without infection.
questions.leadIn: What is the sensitivity of the rapid test?
questions.explanation: Answer: 90%. Why: sensitivity is the share of people with the disease who test positive: true positives / (true positives + false negatives). Here 180 of the 200 infected patients test positive, so sensitivity = 180 / 200 = 90%. The other numbers in the table: specificity = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives) = 760 / 800 = 95%. Positive predictive value = 180 / (180 + 40) = 82%. Negative predictive value = 760 / (760 + 20) = 97%. Predictive values change with disease prevalence; likelihood ratios, like sensitivity and specificity, do not.

whyWrong.a: 10% is the false-negative rate (20 / 200), the share of infected patients the test misses.
whyWrong.b: 82% is the positive predictive value: 180 true positives out of 220 positive tests.
whyWrong.d: 95% is the specificity: 760 of the 800 uninfected patients test negative.
whyWrong.e: 97% is the negative predictive value: 760 true negatives out of 780 negative tests.

sources.title: StatPearls: Diagnostic Testing Accuracy: Sensitivity, Specificity, Predictive Values and Likelihood Ratios

questions.stem: A city starts screening adult smokers for lung cancer with yearly low-dose CT. Five years later, the average survival measured from the date of diagnosis is 2 years longer in screen-detected patients than in patients diagnosed after symptoms began in the years before screening. Tumors found by screening grew at the same rate as those found after symptoms. The lung cancer death rate per 100,000 smokers and the average age at death from lung cancer have not changed.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best explains the longer survival after diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Answer: lead-time bias. Why: lead-time bias occurs when testing detects a disease at an earlier stage, which makes survival look longer even if the patient dies at the same time. Here the clock simply starts earlier: survival from diagnosis rises, but the age at death and the death rate do not change. To avoid it, investigators look at overall mortality from the disease rather than survival from diagnosis, or adjust survival curves by subtracting the estimated lead time.

whyWrong.b: Length-time bias happens when screening mostly finds slow-growing, less dangerous cases. Here the screen-detected tumors grew at the same rate as the others.
whyWrong.c: Selection bias happens when the study group does not represent the target population. The stem gives no sign of that, and it would not explain the unchanged death rate.
whyWrong.d: Recall bias is error from differences in how people remember past events, a problem of questionnaires and case-control studies, not of survival times.
whyWrong.e: The Hawthorne effect is a change in subjects' behavior because they know they are being observed.

questions.topic: Hypothesis testing: type I and type II errors
questions.stem: A randomized trial enrolls 40 patients with heart failure to compare a new drug with placebo. Hospitalization rates are 30% with the drug and 40% with placebo (p = 0.45), and the authors conclude that the drug has no effect. Five years later, a well-designed trial of 4,000 similar patients finds that the drug clearly lowers hospitalizations by a similar amount (p < 0.001).
questions.leadIn: Which of the following best describes the conclusion of the first trial?
questions.explanation: Answer: type II error. Why: a type II error is concluding that there is no difference between groups when a difference really exists (a false negative). The first trial was too small to detect a real 10-point drop in hospitalizations. Statistical power, the ability to correctly reject a null hypothesis that is false, depends on the significance level, the effect size, and above all the sample size. A larger trial raises power and lowers the chance of a type II error.

whyWrong.b: A type I error is the opposite: wrongly reporting a significant difference when none exists (a false positive). The first trial found no difference.
whyWrong.c: Confounding is a third variable that influences both the exposure and the outcome. Randomization limits confounding, and it does not explain a missed real effect in a tiny trial.
whyWrong.d: Recall bias comes from people remembering past events differently. Hospitalizations in a trial are recorded, not recalled.
whyWrong.e: Observer bias is a systematic difference between true and recorded values because of the observer. Hospitalization is an objective outcome, and the problem here is too few patients.

sources.title: StatPearls: Type I and Type II Errors and Statistical Power

questions.stem: Investigators study whether a medication taken in early pregnancy is linked to a heart defect. They identify 300 mothers of infants born with the defect and 600 mothers of healthy infants. Two years after delivery, all mothers complete a questionnaire about medications they took during pregnancy. Mothers of affected infants report many more medications than mothers of healthy infants.
questions.leadIn: Which of the following changes would best reduce the most likely bias in this study?

options.text: Use a stricter p-value cutoff of 0.01
Blind the statisticians to group membership
Match mothers by age and parity

questions.explanation: Answer: verify the answers against pharmacy (and prenatal) records. Why: this is a case-control study, and the most likely problem is recall bias, error from differences between what people remember and what really happened. Mothers of an affected infant have often thought hard about what might have caused it, so they remember exposures more completely than mothers of healthy infants. Recall bias is reduced by corroborating subjective answers with medical records or other objective measures, and by shortening the time between exposure and data collection.

whyWrong.b: A bigger sample makes the estimate more precise, but the same difference in remembering is built into every answer, so the bias stays.
whyWrong.c: A stricter p-value cutoff lowers the chance of a type I error from random chance. It does nothing about a systematic difference in reporting.
whyWrong.d: Blinding reduces observer bias in the people who collect or judge the data. Here the error comes from the mothers' memories.
whyWrong.e: Matching controls for confounding by age and parity. It does not fix differences in how the two groups remember their medications.

questions.topic: Motor neuron disease: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has had progressive weakness for 8 months. He has trouble buttoning his shirt and turning keys, and his legs feel stiff. The muscles of his right hand are wasted, and fasciculations are seen in both forearms and thighs. Muscle tone in the legs is increased, and the knee and ankle reflexes are brisk. Sensation is normal, eye movements are full, and bladder function is normal. Sensory nerve action potentials are normal on nerve conduction studies.
questions.leadIn: Degeneration of which of the following is the most likely cause of his findings?
questions.explanation: Answer: both upper and lower motor neurons (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, ALS). Why: the hallmark of ALS is upper and lower motor neuron signs together. Upper motor neuron signs are spasticity, hyperreflexia, poor dexterity, and incoordination; lower motor neuron signs are muscle atrophy and fasciculations. Sensation is spared, so sensory nerve action potentials are normal, and eye and sphincter muscles are spared until late. Gene testing looks especially for SOD1 and C9ORF72. Riluzole is thought to reduce glutamate-induced excitotoxicity, and edaravone is a free radical scavenger. Median survival is 3 to 5 years, and aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure are the most common causes of death.

whyWrong.b: Lower motor neuron loss alone (as in polio) causes atrophy, fasciculations, and reduced reflexes. It would not explain his spasticity and brisk reflexes.
whyWrong.c: Upper motor neuron damage alone causes spasticity and brisk reflexes, but not muscle wasting or fasciculations.
whyWrong.d: Loss of dorsal root ganglion neurons causes sensory loss. His sensation and sensory nerve studies are normal.
whyWrong.e: Damage to peripheral nerve myelin (as in Guillain-Barre syndrome) causes weakness with absent or reduced reflexes and often sensory symptoms.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated boy living in an area with a poliovirus outbreak had fever, sore throat, and diarrhea 10 days ago. Three days ago he developed muscle pain and then weakness of his left leg. Today the left leg is limp, with decreased tone and an absent knee reflex. The right leg and both arms are normal. Sensation is intact throughout, and he is alert and oriented.
questions.leadIn: Destruction of which of the following cells is the most likely cause of his weakness?

options.text: Upper motor neurons in the motor cortex

questions.explanation: Answer: anterior horn motor neurons (paralytic poliomyelitis). Why: poliovirus, an enterovirus spread by the fecal-oral and oral-oral routes, can destroy the alpha motor neurons in the anterior horns of the spinal cord. The result is asymmetric flaccid weakness, legs more often than arms, with decreased or absent tendon reflexes and no sensory or cognitive deficits. These are lower motor neuron signs. A negative CSF test for poliovirus does not rule out polio. The inactivated vaccine (IPV) carries no risk of vaccine-associated paralytic polio, which the live oral vaccine (OPV) can rarely cause. Years later, some survivors develop new weakness and fatigue (post-polio syndrome).

whyWrong.b: Upper motor neuron damage causes spasticity and brisk reflexes, the opposite of his limp leg with an absent reflex.
whyWrong.c: Dorsal root ganglion neurons carry sensation. His sensation is intact.
whyWrong.d: Immune damage to Schwann cells and myelin is Guillain-Barre syndrome, which typically causes ascending, symmetric weakness, often with sensory symptoms.
whyWrong.e: A primary muscle disease usually causes symmetric weakness of proximal muscles. One limp leg with lost reflexes after a febrile illness points to motor neuron loss.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman is in the hospital 2 days after surgery for a hip fracture. She was alert and oriented before surgery. Tonight she is confused, picks at her bedsheets, and cannot say the months of the year backward. She was given an over-the-counter sleep aid containing diphenhydramine at bedtime for the past 2 nights. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F) and pulse 112/min. Her skin is warm, flushed, and dry, and her pupils are dilated. A bladder scan shows 750 mL of urine.
questions.leadIn: Blockade of which of the following receptors best explains her symptoms?
questions.explanation: Answer: muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Why: acute confusion with inattention after surgery is delirium, and here the cause is the drug. Diphenhydramine is also an antimuscarinic: it competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Blocking them centrally causes delirium and confusion. Blocking them peripherally causes the classic picture: dry skin ("dry as a bone"), flushing ("red as a beet"), fever ("hot as a hare"), dilated pupils and blurred vision, urinary retention ("full as a flask"), and a fast heart rate. Older adults are the most sensitive to anticholinergic drugs, and the American Geriatrics Society says diphenhydramine should generally be avoided in them. Treatment is to stop the drug; physostigmine is an antidote, but its use is debated.

whyWrong.b: Beta-1 blockade slows the heart. Her pulse is fast, and beta-1 blockade does not cause dry skin, dilated pupils, or urinary retention.
whyWrong.c: Dopamine D2 blockade by antipsychotics causes stiffness and other movement problems, not dry skin, dilated pupils, and a full bladder.
whyWrong.d: Alpha-1 blockade lowers blood pressure, especially on standing, and does not cause dry skin or urinary retention.
whyWrong.e: 5-HT3 blockade (for example by ondansetron) is used against nausea and does not cause this anticholinergic picture.

sources.title: StatPearls: Differentiating Delirium Versus Dementia in Older Adults

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has been confused for 2 days. Until last week he lived alone, managed his own money, and drove. His daughter says he is drowsy and hard to keep awake in the morning but agitated at night, and he says he sees bugs crawling on the wall. He cannot keep his attention on a conversation. Temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Urinalysis shows many white blood cells and bacteria.
questions.leadIn: An EEG is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Focal spikes over one temporal lobe

questions.explanation: Answer: generalized slowing. Why: confusion that starts over days, with poor attention, a level of alertness that changes through the day, and visual hallucinations, is delirium, here likely from a urinary tract infection, a common cause in older adults. Inattention and reduced arousal separate delirium from dementia. Dementia develops gradually and patients stay awake, while delirium is acute and fluctuating and often reversible once the cause is treated. Generalized slowing of brain waves on EEG is strongly associated with delirium. In an older adult, new visual hallucinations should be treated as delirium unless proven otherwise.

whyWrong.b: Generalized EEG slowing is strongly associated with delirium, so a normal background would argue against it.
whyWrong.c: Bilateral 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges are the pattern of absence seizures, usually in children aged 5 to 15.
whyWrong.d: Periodic sharp wave complexes are seen in most patients with sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus over months.
whyWrong.e: Focal temporal spikes suggest a seizure focus in one area, not the whole-brain dysfunction of delirium.
